{{Short description|Relativistic quantum mechanical wave equation}}

{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2019}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs1}}
{{Quantum mechanics|cTopic=Equations}}In [[particle physics]], the '''Dirac equation''' is a [[relativistic wave equation]] derived by British physicist [[Paul Dirac]] in 1928.<ref name="Dirac">{{cite journal |last1=Dirac |first1=P. A. M.|author-link1=Paul Dirac|doi=10.1098/rspa.1928.0023|title=The Quantum Theory of the Electron|year=1928|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences|volume=117|issue=778|pages=610–624|bibcode = 1928RSPSA.117..610D|url=http://www.math.ucsd.edu/~nwallach/Dirac1928.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150102071809/http://www.math.ucsd.edu/~nwallach/Dirac1928.pdf |archive-date=2015-01-02 |url-status=live| jstor=94981 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In its [[Dirac equation#Covariant form and relativistic invariance|free form]], or including electromagnetic interactions, it describes all [[spin-1/2|spin-{{sfrac|1|2}}]] [[massive particle]]s, called "Dirac particles", such as [[electron]]s and [[quark]]s for which [[Parity (physics)|parity]] is a [[symmetry (physics)|symmetry]]. It is consistent with both the principles of [[quantum mechanics]] and the theory of [[special relativity]],<ref>{{cite book|title = Quanta: A handbook of concepts|author = P.W. Atkins|publisher=Oxford University Press | page=52 | year = 1974|isbn = 978-0-19-855493-6}}</ref> and was the first theory to fully account for special relativity in the context of quantum mechanics. The equation is validated by its rigorous accounting of the observed [[fine structure]] of the [[Hydrogen spectral series|hydrogen spectrum]] and has become vital in the building of the [[Standard Model]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gorbar |first1=Eduard V. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=heIZEAAAQBAJ&dq=dirac+equation+most+fundamental+equation&pg=PA1 |title=Electronic Properties of Dirac and Weyl Semimetals |last2=Miranskij |first2=Vladimir A. |last3=Shovkovy |first3=Igor A. |last4=Sukhachov |first4=Pavlo O. |publisher=[[World Scientific Publishing]] |year=2021 |isbn=978-981-12-0736-5 |location= |pages=1 |language=en}}</ref>

The equation also implied the existence of a new form of matter, ''[[antimatter]]'', previously unsuspected and unobserved. 
The existence of antimatter was experimentally confirmed several years later. It also provided a ''theoretical'' justification for the introduction of several component wave functions in [[Wolfgang Pauli|Pauli]]'s [[phenomenology (particle physics)|phenomenological]] theory of [[Spin (physics)|spin]]. The wave functions in the Dirac theory are vectors of four [[complex number]]s (known as [[Dirac spinor]]s), two of which resemble [[Pauli equation|the Pauli wavefunction]] in the non-relativistic limit, in contrast to the [[Schrödinger equation]], which described wave functions of only one complex value. Moreover, in the limit of zero mass, the Dirac equation reduces to the [[Weyl equation]]. In the context of [[quantum field theory]], the Dirac equation is reinterpreted to describe quantum fields corresponding to spin-{{sfrac|1|2}} particles.

Dirac did not fully appreciate the importance of his results; however, the entailed explanation of spin as a consequence of the union of quantum mechanics and relativity—and the eventual discovery of the [[positron]]—represents one of the great triumphs of [[theoretical physics]]. This accomplishment has been described as fully on par with the works of [[Isaac Newton]], [[James Clerk Maxwell]], and [[Albert Einstein]] before him.<ref>{{cite book|title=The New Quantum Universe|author=T.Hey, P.Walters|publisher = Cambridge University Press|year=2009|page = 228|isbn = 978-0-521-56457-1}}</ref> The equation has been deemed by some physicists to be "the real seed of modern physics".<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Zichichi |first=Antonino |author-link=Antonino Zichichi |date=2000-03-02 |title=Dirac, Einstein and physics |url=https://physicsworld.com/a/dirac-einstein-and-physics/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=Physics World |language=en-GB}}</ref> The Dirac equation has been described as the "centerpiece of relativistic quantum mechanics", and as "perhaps the most important [equation] in all of quantum mechanics".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Han |first=Moo-Young |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_AC3CgAAQBAJ&pg=PA32 |title=From Photons to Higgs: A Story of Light |publisher=[[World Scientific Publishing]] |year=2014 |isbn=978-981-4579-95-7 |edition=2nd |pages=32 |language=en |doi=10.1142/9071}}</ref>

== History ==

=== Early attempts at a relativistic formulation ===

The first phase in the development of [[quantum mechanics]], lasting between 1900 and 1925, focused on explaining individual phenomena that could not be explained through [[classical mechanics]].<ref>{{cite book|last=ter Haar|first=D.|author-link=Dirk ter Haar|date=1967|title=The Old Quantum Theory|url=|doi=10.1016/B978-0-08-012102-4.50003-6|location=|publisher=Pergamon|chapter=|page=1|isbn=978-0-08-012102-4}}</ref> The second phase, starting in the mid-1920s, saw the development of two systematic frameworks governing quantum mechanics. The first, known as [[matrix mechanics]], uses [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] to describe [[observable|physical observables]]; it was developed in 1925 by [[Werner Heisenberg]], [[Max Born]], and [[Pascual Jordan]].<ref name="BJBook">{{cite book|last1=Bransden|first1=B.H.|author-link1=|last2=Joachain|first2=C.J.|author-link2=Charles J. Joachain|date=2000|title=Quantum Mechanics|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Pearson|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0582356917}}</ref>{{rp|51}} The second, known as wave mechanics, uses a [[wave equation]] known as the [[Schrödinger equation]] to describe the [[quantum state|state]] of a [[physical system|system]]; it was developed the next year by [[Erwin Schrödinger]].  While these two frameworks were initially seen as competing approaches, they would later be shown to be equivalent.<ref name="BCKBook">{{cite book|last1=Bialynicki-Birula|first1=I.|author-link1=Iwo Białynicki-Birula|last2=Cieplak|first2=M.|author-link2=|last3=Kaminski|first3=J.|author-link3=|date=1992|title=Theory of Quanta|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Oxford University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0195071573}}</ref>{{rp|21}}

Both these frameworks only formulated quantum mechanics in a [[special relativity|non-relativistic]] setting.<ref name="BCKBook"/>{{rp|22}} This was seen as a deficiency right from the start, with Schrödinger originally attempting to formulate a [[Relativistic wave equations|relativistic version]] of the Schrödinger equation, in the process discovering the [[Klein–Gordon equation]].<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|679}} However, after showing that this [[equation]] did not correctly reproduce the relativistic corrections to the [[hydrogen atom]] [[emission spectrum|spectrum]] for which an exact form was known due to [[Arnold Sommerfeld]], he abandoned his [[theory of relativity|relativistic formulation]].<ref name="KGHis">{{cite journal|last1=Kragh|first1=H.|authorlink1=Helge Kragh|date=1984|title=Equation with the many fathers. The Klein-Gordon equation in 1926|url=|journal=American Journal of Physics|volume=52|issue=11|pages=1024–1033|doi=10.1119/1.13782|pmid=|arxiv=|s2cid=|access-date=}}</ref>{{rp|1025}} The Klein–Gordon equation was also found by at least six other authors in the same year.<ref name="His2">{{cite journal|last1=Tsutsui|first1=T.T.|authorlink1=|last2=Silva|first2=E.O.|authorlink2=|last3=M de Castro|first3=A.S.|authorlink3=|last4=Andrade|first4=F.M.|authorlink4=|date=2025|title=The Dirac equation: historical context, comparisons with the Schrödinger and Klein-Gordon equations, and elementary consequences|url=|journal=European Journal of Physics|volume=46|issue=5|pages=053001|doi=10.1088/1361-6404/adf9a5|pmid=|arxiv=2504.17797|s2cid=|access-date=}}</ref>{{rp|6}}

During 1926 and 1927, there was a widespread effort to incorporate relativity into quantum mechanics, largely through two approaches. The first was to consider the Klein–Gordon as the correct relativistic generalization of the Schrödinger equation.<ref name="His2"/>{{rp|7}} Such an approach was viewed unfavourably by many leading [[physicist|theorists]] since it failed to correctly predict numerous [[experimental data|experimental results]], and more importantly it appeared difficult to reconcile with the principles of quantum mechanics as understood at the time.<ref name="History">{{cite journal|last1=Kragh|first1=H.|authorlink1=Helge Kragh|date=1981|title=The genesis of dirac's relativistic theory of electrons|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00327714|journal=Archive for History of Exact Sciences|volume=24|issue=1|pages=31–67|doi=10.1007/BF00327714|pmid=|arxiv=|s2cid=|access-date=|url-access=subscription}}</ref>{{rp|35}} These conceptual issues primarily arose due to the presence of a [[second derivative|second temporal derivative]].<ref name="KGHis"/>{{rp|1031}}

The second approach introduced relativistic effects as corrections to the known non-relativistic formulas.<ref name="History"/>{{rp|36}} This provided many provisional answers that were expected to eventually be supplanted by some yet-unknown relativistic formulation of quantum mechanics. One notable result by Heisenberg and Jordan was the introduction of two terms for [[spin (physics)|spin]] and relativity into the hydrogen [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]], allowing them to derive the [[order of approximation|first-order approximation]] of the Sommerfeld [[fine structure]] formula.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Heisenberg|first1=W.|authorlink1=Werner Heisenberg|last2=Jordan|first2=P.|authorlink2=Pascual Jordan|date=1926|title=Anwendung der Quantenmechanik auf das Problem der anomalen Zeemaneffekte|url=|journal=Zeitschrift für Physik|volume=37|issue=4|pages=263–277|doi=10.1007/BF01397100|pmid=|arxiv=|s2cid=|access-date=}}</ref>

A parallel development during this time was the concept of spin, first introduced in 1925 by [[Samuel Goudsmit]] and [[George Uhlenbeck]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Uhlenbeck, G. |first1=G. |author-link1=George Uhlenbeck |last2=Goudsmit |first2=S. |author-link2=Samuel Goudsmit|date=November 1925 |title=Ersetzung der Hypothese vom unmechanischen Zwang durch eine Forderung bezüglich des inneren Verhaltens jedes einzelnen Elektrons |journal=Die Naturwissenschaften |language=de |volume=13 |issue=47 |pages=953–954 |doi=10.1007/bf01558878 |issn=0028-1042 |s2cid=32211960}}</ref> Shortly after, it was conjectured by Schrödinger to be the missing link in acquiring the correct Sommerfeld formula.<ref name="History"/>{{rp|44}} In 1927, [[Wolfgang Pauli]] used the ideas of spin to find an [[effective theory]] for a nonrelativistic [[spin-1/2|spin-{{sfrac|1|2}}]] [[particle]], the [[Pauli equation]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Pauli|first=Wolfgang|author-link=Wolfgang Pauli|year=1927|title=Zur Quantenmechanik des magnetischen Elektrons|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01397326|journal=Zeitschrift für Physik|language=de|volume=43|issue=9–10|pages=601–623|doi=10.1007/BF01397326|bibcode=1927ZPhy...43..601P|s2cid=128228729|issn=0044-3328|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He did this by taking the Schrödinger equation and, rather than just assuming that the wave function depends on the [[coordinate system|physical coordinate]], he also assumed that it depends on a spin coordinate that can take only two values <math>\pm \tfrac{\hbar}{2}</math>. While this was still a non-relativistic formulation, he believed that a fully relativistic formulation possibly required a more complicated model for the [[electron]], one that moved beyond a [[point particle]].<ref name="History"/>{{rp|47}}

=== Dirac's relativistic quantum mechanics ===

By 1927, many physicists no longer considered the fine structure of hydrogen as a crucial puzzle that called for a completely new relativistic formulation since it could effectively be solved using the Pauli equation or by introducing a spin-{{sfrac|1|2}} [[angular momentum]] [[quantum number]] in the Klein–Gordon equation.<ref name="History"/>{{rp|51}} At the fifth [[Solvay Conference]] held that year, [[Paul Dirac]] was primarily concerned with the logical development of quantum mechanics. However, he realized that many other physicists complacently accepted the Klein–Gordon equation as a satisfactory relativistic formulation, which demanded abandoning basic principles of quantum mechanics as understood at the time, to which Dirac strongly objected.<ref name="History"/>{{rp|52}} After his return from [[Brussels]], Dirac focused on finding a relativistic theory for electrons. Within two months he solved the problem and published his results on January 2, 1928.<ref name="Dirac"/>

In his [[Academic publishing#Scholarly paper|paper]], Dirac was guided by two principles from [[transformation theory (quantum mechanics)|transformation theory]], the first being that the equation should be [[invariant (physics)|invariant]] under transformations of special relativity, and the second that it should transform under the transformation theory of quantum mechanics.<ref name="His2"/>{{rp|9}} The latter demanded that the equation would have to be [[linearity|linear]] in [[time derivative|temporal derivatives]], so that it would admit a [[Born rule|probabilistic interpretation]]. His argument begins with the Klein–Gordon equation<ref name="Schwartz">{{cite book|first=M. D.|last=Schwartz|title=Quantum Field Theory and the Standard Model|publisher=Cambridge University Press|date=2014|chapter=|page=|isbn=9781107034730}}</ref>{{rp|32}}

:<math>
\left[\boldsymbol p^2+m^2c^2\right]\phi(t,x) = -\frac{\hbar^2}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2} \phi(t,x),
</math>

describing a particle using the wave function <math>\phi(t,x)</math>. Here <math>\boldsymbol p^2 = p_1^2+p_2^2+p_3^2</math> is the square of the [[momentum]], <math>m</math> is the [[invariant mass|rest mass]] of the particle, <math>c</math> is the [[speed of light]], and <math>\hbar</math> is the [[Planck constant|reduced Planck constant]]. The naive way to get an equation linear in the time derivative is to essentially consider the [[square root]] of both sides. This replaces <math>\boldsymbol p^2+m^2c^2</math> with <math>\sqrt{\boldsymbol p^2+m^2c^2}</math>. However, such a [[matrix square root|square root]] is mathematically problematic for the resulting theory, making it unfeasible.<ref name="BCKBook"/>{{rp|379}}

Dirac's first insight was the concept of linearization. He looked for some sort of [[variable (mathematics)|variables]] <math>\alpha_i</math> that are independent of momentum and spacetime coordinates for which the square root could be rewritten in a linear form<ref name="BCKBook"/>{{rp|379}}

:<math>
\sqrt{p_1^2+p_2^2+p_3^2+(mc)^2} = \alpha_1p_1+\alpha_2p_2+\alpha_3p_3+\alpha_4 mc.
</math>

By squaring this [[operator (physics)|operator]] and demanding that it reduces to the Klein–Gordon equation, Dirac found that the variables must satisfy <math>\alpha_i^2=1</math> and <math>\alpha_i\alpha_j + \alpha_j\alpha_i=0</math> if <math>i \neq j</math>. Dirac initially considered the <math>2\times 2</math> [[Pauli matrices]] as a candidate, but then showed these would not work since it is impossible to find a set of four <math>2\times 2</math> matrices that all [[anticommutative property|anticommute]] with each other.<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|687}} His second insight was to instead consider [[dimension (vector space)|four-dimensional]] matrices. In that case the equation would be acting on a [[vector (mathematics and physics)|four-component]] wavefunction <math>\psi = (\psi_1, \psi_2, \psi_3, \psi_4)</math>.<ref name="Davyadov">{{cite book|last=Davydov|first=A.S.|author-link=Alexander Davydov (physicist)|date=1976|title=Quantum Mechanics|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Pergamon Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0080204383}}</ref>{{rp|235}} Such a proposal was much more bold than Pauli's original generalization to a two-component wavefunction in the Pauli equation.<ref name="History"/>{{rp|57}} This is because in Pauli's case, this was motivated by the demand to encode the two spin states of the particle. In contrast, Dirac had no physical argument for a four-component wavefunction, but instead introduced it as a matter of mathematical necessity. When the quantum mechanical momentum operators are substituted for the classical momentum he arrived at what we call the Dirac equation<ref>{{cite book |last=Thaller |first=Bernd |title=The Dirac Equation |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |date=2013 |isbn=978-3-662-02753-0 |doi=10.1007/978-3-662-02753-0 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Dirac_Equation/4bftCAAAQBAJ}}</ref>{{rp|2}}

:<math>
\left( i\hbar \mathbf{\alpha}\cdot\mathbf{\nabla} + \beta mc\right)  \mathbf{\psi}(t,x)= i\frac{\hbar}{c}\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \mathbf{\psi}(t,x).
</math>
where the wave functions are now 4 dimensional vectors.
Dirac constructed the correct matrices <math>\alpha_i</math> without realizing that they form a mathematical structure known of since the early 1880s, the [[Clifford algebra]].<ref name="Lounesto">{{cite book|last=Lounesto|first=P.|author-link=|date=1997|title=Clifford Algebras and Spinors|series=London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series, Series Number 239|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Cambridge University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0521599160}}</ref>{{rp|320}} By recasting the equation in a [[Lorentz covariance|Lorentz invariant]] form, he also showed that it correctly combines special relativity with his principle of quantum mechanical transformation theory, making it a viable candidate for a relativistic theory of the electron.<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|685}}

To investigate the equation further, he examined how it behaves in the presence of an [[electromagnetic field]].<ref name="History"/>{{rp|58}} To his surprise, this showed that it described a particle with a [[magnetic moment]] arising due to the particle having spin {{sfrac|1|2}}. Spin directly emerged from the equation, without Dirac having added it in by hand. Additionally, he focused on showing that the equation successfully reproduces the fine structure of the hydrogen atom, at least to first order. The equation therefore succeeds where all previous attempts have failed, in correctly describing relativistic phenomena of electrons from [[first principle]]s rather than through the ad hoc modification of existing formulas.<ref name="History"/>{{rp|60}}

=== Consequences ===
Except for his followup paper<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Dirac|first1=P.|authorlink1=Paul Dirac|date=1928|title=The Quantum theory of electron. 2.|url=|journal=Proc. Roy. Soc. Lond. A|volume=118|issue=|pages=351|doi=10.1098/rspa.1928.0056|pmid=|arxiv=|s2cid=|access-date=|doi-access=free}}</ref> deriving the [[Zeeman effect]] and Paschen–Back effect from the equation in the presences of a [[magnetic field]]s, Dirac left the work of examining the consequences of his equation to others, and only came back to the subject in 1930.<ref name="History"/>{{rp|65}} Once the equation was published, it was recognized as the correct solution to the problem of spin, relativity, and quantum mechanics. At first the Dirac equation was considered the only valid relativistic equation for a particle with [[mass]]. Then in 1934 Pauli and [[Victor Weisskopf]] reinterpreted the Klein–Gordon equation as the equation for a relativistic [[scalar boson|spinless particle]].<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|685}}

One of the first calculations was to reproduce the Sommerfeld fine structure formula exactly, which was performed independently by [[Charles Galton Darwin]] and [[Walter Gordon (physicist)|Walter Gordon]] in 1928.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Gordon|first1=W.|authorlink1=Walter Gordon (physicist)|date=1928|title=Die Energieniveaus des Wasserstoffatoms nach der Diracschen Quantentheorie des Elektrons|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01351570|journal=Zeitschrift für Physik|volume=48|issue=1|pages=11–14|doi=10.1007/BF01351570|pmid=|arxiv=|bibcode=1928ZPhy...48...11G |s2cid=|access-date=|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Darwin|first1=C.G.|authorlink1=Charles Galton Darwin|date=1928|title=The wave equations of the electron|url=|journal=Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A|volume=118|issue=780|pages=654–680|doi=10.1098/rspa.1928.0076|pmid=|arxiv=|s2cid=|access-date=|doi-access=free |bibcode=1928RSPSA.118..654D }}</ref><ref name="BCKBook"/>{{rp|377}} This is the first time that the full formula has been derived from first principles. Further work on the mathematics of the equation was undertaken by [[Hermann Weyl]] in 1929.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Weyl|first1=H.|authorlink1=Hermann Weyl|date=1929|title=Elektron und Gravitation. I|url=|journal=Zeitschrift für Physik|volume=56|issue=5|pages=330–352|doi=10.1007/BF01339504|pmid=|arxiv=|bibcode=1929ZPhy...56..330W |s2cid=|access-date=}}</ref> In this work he showed that the [[massless particle|massless]] Dirac equation can be decomposed into a pair of [[Weyl equation]]s.

The Dirac equation was also used to study various scattering processes. In particular, the [[Klein–Nishina formula]], looking at [[photon]]-electron [[scattering]], was also derived in 1928.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/BF01366453 |last1=Klein|first1=O.|authorlink1=Oskar Klein|last2=Nishina|first2=Y.|authorlink2=Yoshio Nishina|title=Über die Streuung von Strahlung durch freie Elektronen nach der neuen relativistischen Quantendynamik von Dirac|journal=Z. Phys.|volume=52 |issue=11–12 |year=1929|pages=853 and 869|bibcode = 1929ZPhy...52..853K |s2cid=123905506 }}</ref> [[Mott scattering]], the scattering of electrons off a heavy target such as [[atomic nucleus|atomic nuclei]], followed the next year.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Mott|first1=N.F.|authorlink1=Nevill Mott|date=1929|title=The Scattering of Fast Electrons by Atomic Nuclei|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Containing Papers of a Mathematical and Physical Character|volume=124|issue=794|pages=425–442|doi=10.1098/rspa.1929.0127|pmid=|arxiv=|s2cid=|doi-access=free |jstor=95377 |bibcode=1929RSPSA.124..425M }}</ref> Over the following years it was further used to derive other standard scattering processes such as [[Moller scattering]] in 1932<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Møller|first1=C.|authorlink1=Christian Møller|date=1932|title=Zur Theorie des Durchgangs schneller Elektronen durch Materie|url=https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19324060506|journal= Annalen der Physik|volume=406|issue=5|pages=531–585|doi=10.1002/andp.19324060506|pmid=|arxiv=|bibcode=1932AnP...406..531M |s2cid=|access-date=|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and [[Bhabha scattering]] in 1936.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bhabha|first1=H.J.|authorlink1=Homi J. Bhabha|date=1936|title=The scattering of positrons by electrons with exchange on Dirac's theory of the positron|url=http://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1936.0046|journal=Proc. R. Soc. Lond.|volume=154|issue=881|pages=195–206|doi=10.1098/rspa.1936.0046|pmid=|arxiv=|bibcode=1936RSPSA.154..195B |s2cid=|access-date=|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

A problem that gained more focus with time was the presence of [[negative energy]] [[quantum state|states]] in the Dirac equation, which led to many efforts to try to eliminate such states. Dirac initially simply rejected the negative energy states as unphysical,<ref name="History"/>{{rp|63}} but the problem was made more clear when in 1929 [[Oskar Klein]] showed that in static fields there exists inevitable mixing between the negative and positive energy states.<ref name="BCKBook"/>{{rp|378}} Dirac's initial response was to believe that his equation must have some sort of defect, and that it was only the first approximation of a future theory that would not have this problem.<ref name="BCKBook"/>{{rp|378}} However, he then suggested a solution to the problem in the form of the [[Dirac sea]]. This is the idea that the universe is filled with an infinite sea of negative energy electrons states. Positive energy electron states then live in this sea and are prevented from decaying to the negative energy states through the [[Pauli exclusion principle]].<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|715}}

Additionally, Dirac postulated the existence of positively charged [[Dirac hole theory|holes]] in the Dirac sea, which he initially suggested could be the [[proton]]. However, Oppenheimer showed that in this case stable [[atom]]s could not exist<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Oppenheimer|first1=J.R.|authorlink1=|date=1930|title=On the Theory of Electrons and Protons|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.35.562|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume=35|issue=5|pages=562–563|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.35.562|pmid=|arxiv=|bibcode=1930PhRv...35..562O |s2cid=|access-date=|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and Weyl further showed that the holes would have to have the same mass as the electrons.<ref>{{cite book|last=Weyl|first=H.|author-link=Hermann Weyl|date=1931|title=The Theory of Groups and Quantum Mechanics|doi=|location=|publisher=Dover Publications|chapter=|page=263|isbn=|url=https://ia601500.us.archive.org/23/items/in.ernet.dli.2015.176925/2015.176925.The-Theory-Of-Groups-And-Quantom-Mechanics.pdf}}</ref> Persuaded by Oppenheimer's and Weyl's argument, Dirac published a paper in 1931 that predicted the existence of an as-yet-unobserved particle that he called an "anti-electron" that would have the same mass and the opposite charge as an electron and that would mutually annihilate upon contact with an electron. He suggested that every particle may have an oppositely charged partner, a concept now called [[antimatter]]<ref>
{{cite journal
 |last=Dirac |first=P. A. M.
 |author-link=Paul Dirac
 |year=1931
 |title=Quantised Singularities in the Quantum Field
 |journal=[[Proceedings of the Royal Society A]]
 |volume=133 |issue=821 |pages=60–72
 |bibcode=1931RSPSA.133...60D
 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1931.0130
 |doi-access=free
}}</ref><ref>{{cite book
 |last=Close |first=F. E.
 |date=2009
 |title=Antimatter
 |page=114
 |publisher=Oxford University Press
 |isbn=978-0-19-955016-6
}}</ref>{{rp|47}}

In 1933 [[Carl David Anderson|Carl Anderson]] discovered the "positive electron", now called a [[positron]], which had all the properties of Dirac's anti-electron.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anderson |first1=Carl|year=1933|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.43.491|title=The Positive Electron|journal=Physical Review|volume=43|issue=6|page=491|bibcode = 1933PhRv...43..491A |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="BCKBook"/>{{rp|378}} While the Dirac sea was later superseded by [[quantum field theory]], its conceptual legacy survived in the idea of a [[quantum vacuum state|dynamical vacuum]] filled with [[virtual particle]]s.<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|717}} In 1949 [[Ernst Stueckelberg]] suggested and [[Richard Feynman]] showed in detail that the negative energy solutions can be interpreted as particles traveling backwards in [[proper time]].<ref name="Blundell"/>{{rp|61–63}}<ref name="BCKBook"/>{{rp|379}}<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Feynman|first1=R.P.|authorlink1=Richard Feynman|date=1949|title=Space-Time Approach to Quantum Electrodynamics|url=|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume=76|issue=6|pages=769–789|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.76.769|pmid=|arxiv=|bibcode=1949PhRv...76..769F |s2cid=|access-date=}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Feynman|first1=R.P.|authorlink1=Richard Feynman|date=1949|title=The Theory of positrons|url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/3520/|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume=76|issue=6|pages=749–759|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.76.749|pmid=|arxiv=|bibcode=1949PhRv...76..749F |s2cid=|access-date=}}</ref> The concept of the Dirac sea is also realized more explicitly in some [[condensed matter physics|condensed matter systems]] in the form of the [[Fermi sea]], which consists of a sea of filled [[valence electron]]s below some [[chemical potential]].<ref name="ASBook">{{cite book|last1=Altland|first1=A.|author-link1=|last2=Simons|first2=B.|author-link2=Benjamin Simons|date=2023|title=Condensed Matter Field Theory|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Cambridge University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-1108494601}}</ref>{{rp|534}}

Significant work was done over the following decades to try to find [[spectroscopy|spectroscopic]] discrepancies compared to the predictions made by the Dirac equation, however it was not until 1947 that [[Lamb shift]] was discovered, which the equation does not predict.<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|710}} This led to the development of [[quantum electrodynamics]] in the 1950s, with the Dirac equation then being incorporated within the context of quantum field theory.<ref name="Peskin">{{cite book|last1=Peskin|first1=M.E.|author-link1=Michael Peskin|last2=Schroeder|first2=D.V.|author-link2=|date=1995|title=An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=CRC Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0201503975}}</ref>{{rp|35}} Since it describes the dynamics of Dirac spinors, it went on to play a fundamental role in the [[Standard Model]] as well as many other areas of physics. For example, within condensed matter physics, systems whose fermions have a near linear [[dispersion relation]] are described by the Dirac equation. Such systems are known as [[Dirac matter]] and they include [[graphene]] and [[topological insulator]]s, which have become a major area of research since the start of the 21st century.<ref name="ASBook"/>{{rp|522}}

The Dirac equation is inscribed upon a plaque on the floor of [[Westminster Abbey]]. Unveiled on 13 November 1995, the plaque commemorates Dirac's life.<ref>{{cite web|author=Gisela Dirac-Wahrenburg |url=http://www.dirac.ch/PaulDirac.html |title=Paul Dirac |publisher=Dirac.ch |access-date=2013-07-12}}</ref> The equation, in its [[natural units]] formulation, is also prominently displayed in the auditorium at the ‘Paul A.M. Dirac’ Lecture Hall at the Patrick M.S. Blackett Institute (formerly The San Domenico Monastery) of the [[Ettore Majorana Foundation and Centre for Scientific Culture]] in [[Erice]], [[Sicily]].

== Formulation ==

=== Covariant formulation ===

In its modern [[classical field theory|field theoretic]] formulation, the Dirac equation in 3+1 dimensional [[Minkowski spacetime]] is written in terms of a ''Dirac field'' <math>\psi(x)</math>. This is a [[field (physics)|field]] that assigns a [[complex vector]] from <math>\mathbb C^4</math> to each point in [[spacetime]],<ref name="Lounesto"/>{{rp|136}} where the key property of the field is that it transforms as a [[Dirac spinor]] under [[Lorentz transformation]]s.<ref name="Freedman">{{cite book|last1=Freedman|first1=D.Z.|author-link1=Daniel Z. Freedman|last2=Van Proeyen|first2=A.|author-link2=|date=2012|title=Supergravity|url=|doi=|location=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0521194013}}</ref>{{rp|28}} In [[natural units]] where <math>\hbar = c = 1</math>, the [[Lorentz covariant]] formulation of the Dirac equation is given by<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|168}}

{{Equation box 1
|title='''Dirac equation'''
|indent=:
|equation = <math> (i{{\partial}\!\!\!/} - m)\psi(x) = 0, </math>
|border
|border colour =#50C878
|background colour = #ECFCF4
}}

where <math>{{\partial}\!\!\!/} = \gamma^\mu \partial_\mu</math> is a [[tensor contraction|contraction]] between the [[four-gradient]] <math>\partial_\mu</math> and the [[gamma matrices]] <math>\gamma^\mu</math>.{{refn|group=nb|This article uses the [[Einstein notation|Einstein summation convention]], where there is an implicit summation over spacetime coordinates for any pairs of repeated indices.}} These are a set of four matrices [[Generator (mathematics)|generating]] the [[Dirac algebra]], which requires them to satisfy<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|40}}

:<math>
\{ \gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu \} =2\eta^{\mu\nu}I_4,
</math>

where <math>\{a,b\} = ab+ba</math> is the [[commutator|anticommutator]], <math>\eta^{\mu\nu}</math> is the Minkowski [[metric tensor (general relativity)|metric]] in a mainly [[metric signature|negative signature]],{{refn|group=nb|In the mainly negative signature <math>\eta^{\mu\nu}</math> is a [[diagonal matrix]] with +1 for <math>\mu = \nu = 0</math> and -1 for the remaining components.}} and <math>I_4</math> is the <math>4\times4</math> [[identity matrix]]. The Dirac algebra is a special case of the more general mathematical structure known as a [[Clifford algebra]].<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|169}} The Dirac algebra can also be seen as the real part of the [[spacetime algebra]]. There is no unique choice of matrices for the gamma matrices, with different choices known as different [[algebra representation|representations of the algebra]].<ref name="Blundell">{{cite book|last1=Lancaster|first1=T.|author-link1=|last2=Blundell|first2=S.J.|author-link2=Stephen Blundell|date=2015|title=Quantum Field Theory for the Gifted Amateur|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Oxford University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0199699339}}</ref>{{rp|323}} One common choice, originally discovered by Dirac, is known as the Dirac representation. Here the matrices are given by<ref name="ASBook"/>{{rp|531}}

:<math>
\gamma^0 = \begin{pmatrix} I_2 & 0 \\
0 & -I_2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \gamma^i = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma_i \\
- \sigma_i & 0\end{pmatrix},
</math>

where <math>\sigma_i</math> are the three [[Pauli matrices]] for <math>i \in \{1,2,3\}</math>. There are two other common representations for the gamma matrices. The first is the [[chirality (physics)|chiral]] representation, which is useful when decomposing the Dirac equation into a pair of [[Weyl equation]]s.<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|41}} The second is the Majorana representation, for which all gamma matrices are [[imaginary number|imaginary]], so the [[Dirac operator]] is [[real number|purely real]].<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|344}} This representation is useful for studying [[Majorana equation|Majorana spinor]]s, which are purely real four-component [[spinor]] solutions of the Dirac equation.<ref name="ASBook"/>{{rp|536}}

By taking the [[hermitian adjoint|hermitian conjugate]] of the Dirac equation and multiplying it by <math>\gamma^0</math> from the right, the adjoint Dirac equation can be found, with this being the [[equation of motion]] for the [[Dirac adjoint]] <math>\bar \psi = \psi^\dagger \gamma^0</math>. It is given by<ref>{{cite web |last=Boyd|first=S.|date=2020|title=The Dirac Equation|url=https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/physics/staff/academic/boyd/stuff/neutrinolectures/dirac.pdf|website=University of Warwick|location=Warwick|publisher=University of Warwick|access-date=November 15, 2025}}</ref>

:<math>
\bar \psi(x)(-i \gamma^\mu \overleftarrow{\partial}_\mu -m)=0.
</math>

The adjoint spinor is useful in forming Lorentz invariant quantities. For example, the [[Bilinear form|bilinear]] <math>\psi^\dagger \psi</math> is not Lorentz invariant, but <math>\bar \psi \psi</math> is.<ref name="ASBook"/>{{rp|532}} Here <math>\overleftarrow{\partial}_\mu</math> is shorthand notation for a [[partial derivative]] acting on the left. In regular notation, the adjoint Dirac equation is equivalent to<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|43}}

:<math>
-i\partial_\mu \bar \psi(x)\gamma^\mu -m\bar \psi(x)=0.
</math>

The Dirac equation can be rewritten in a non-covariant form similar to that of the [[Schrödinger equation]]<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|686}}

:<math>
i \hbar \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\psi(t,\boldsymbol x) = -i \hbar  c\boldsymbol \alpha \cdot \boldsymbol{\nabla}\psi(t,\boldsymbol x) + \beta mc^2 \psi(t, \boldsymbol x).
</math>

The right-hand side of the equation is the [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] acting on the Dirac spinor <math>H\psi</math>. Here <math>\boldsymbol \alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are a set of four [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian]] <math>4\times 4</math> matrices that all anticommute with each other and square to the identity. They are related to the gamma matrices through <math>\gamma^0 = \beta</math>  and <math>\gamma^i = \beta \alpha_i</math>.<ref name="BCKBook"/>{{rp|375}} This form is useful in [[quantum mechanics]], where the Hamiltonian can be easily modified to solve a wide range of problems, such as by introducing a [[potential energy|potential]]<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|702}} or through a [[minimal coupling]] to the [[electromagnetic field]].<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|688}}

=== Dirac action ===

The Dirac equation can also be acquired from a [[Lagrangian (field theory)|Lagrangian formulation]] of the field theory, where the Dirac [[action (physics)|action]] is given by<ref name="ASBook"/>{{rp|535}}

:<math>
S = \int d^4 x \bar \psi(i{{\partial}\!\!\!/} - m)\psi.
</math>

The equation then arises as the [[Euler–Lagrange equation]] of this action, found by varying the adjoint spinor <math>\bar \psi(x)</math>.<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|43}} Meanwhile, the adjoint Dirac equation is acquired by varying the spinor <math>\psi(x)</math>. The action formulation of the Dirac equation has the advantage of making the [[symmetry (physics)|symmetries]] of the Dirac equation more explicit, since they leave its action invariant.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|166–168}} [[Noether's theorem]] then allows for the direct calculation of [[four-current|currents]] corresponding to these symmetries.<ref name="CFT">{{cite book|last=Năstase |first=H.|author-link=|date=2019|title=Classical Field Theory|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Cambridge University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-1108477017}}</ref>{{rp|166}} Additionally, the action is usually used to define the associated [[quantum field theory]], such as through the [[path integral formulation]].<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|251}}

=== Meaning of the Dirac fields ===
In quantum mechanics, the Dirac spinor <math>\psi(x)</math> corresponds to a four-component spinor [[wave function]] describing the [[quantum state|state]] of a [[Dirac fermion]].<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|685}} Its position [[probability density function|probability density]], the probability of finding the fermion in a region of space, is described by the zeroth component of its vector current, <math>\psi^\dagger \psi</math>.<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|689}} In the case of a large number of [[particle]]s, it can also be interpreted as the [[charge density]].<ref name="Lounesto"/>{{rp|137}} An appropriate [[normalized solution (mathematics)|normalization]] is required to ensure that the total probability across all of space is equal to one, with [[probability current|probability conservation]] following directly from the [[conserved current|conservation]] of the vector current. The Dirac equation is the [[Relativistic wave equations|relativistic]] analogue of the Schrödinger equation for the Dirac fermion wavefunction.

In the [[second quantization]] form of quantum field theory  the Dirac spinor is [[quantization (physics)|quantized]] to be an operator-valued spinor field <math>\hat \psi(x)</math>.<ref name="Stanford">{{cite book|last=Kuhlmann|first=M.|editor-last1=Zalta|editor-first1=E.N.|editor-link1=|editor-last2=Nodelman|editor-first2=U.|editor-link2=|date=2023|title=Quantum Field Theory|doi=|location=|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|edition = Summer 2023|chapter=|page=|url = https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2023/entries/quantum-field-theory/|isbn=}}</ref> In contrast to quantum mechanics, it no longer represents the state in the [[Hilbert space]], but is rather the [[operator (physics)|operator]] that acts on states to create or destroy particles.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|22}}<ref name="Griffiths">{{cite book|last=Griffiths|first=D.J.|author-link=|date=2018|title=Introduction to Quantum Mechanics|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Cambridge University Press|edition=3rd|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-1107189638}}</ref>{{rp|92}} [[Observable]]s are formed using [[correlation function (quantum field theory)|expectation values]] of these operators.<ref name="Kaplan">{{cite web |last=Kaplan|first=J.|date=2016|title=QFT Lectures Notes|url=https://sites.krieger.jhu.edu/jared-kaplan/files/2016/05/QFTNotes.pdf|website=Johns Hopkins Krieger School of Arts and Sciences|location=|publisher=Johns Hopkins University|access-date=November 15, 2025}}</ref>{{rp|41}} The Dirac equation then becomes an operator equation describing the state-independent evolution of the operator-valued spinor field<ref name="Polchinski">{{cite book|last=Polchinski|first=J.|author-link=Joseph Polchinski|date=2005|title=String Theory, Volume I|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Cambridge University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0143113799}}</ref>{{rp|35}}

:<math>
(i{{\partial}\!\!\!/} - m)\hat \psi(x) = 0.
</math>

In the [[path integral formulation]] of quantum field theory, the spinor field <math>\psi(x)</math> is an anti-commuting [[Grassmann number|Grassmann-valued]] field that only acts as an integration variable.<ref name="Freedman"/>{{rp|29}} The Dirac equation then emerges as the classical [[saddle point]] behaviour of the path integral. It also arises as an equation of the expectation value of the classical field variables<ref name="Polchinski"/>{{rp|35}}

:<math>
\langle (i{{\partial}\!\!\!/} - m)\psi(x)\rangle = 0,
</math>

in the sense of the [[Schwinger–Dyson equation]]s.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|80}} This version of the equation can also be acquired by taking the expectation value of the operator equation.

The Dirac equation also arises in describing the [[time evolution]] of a spinor field in [[classical field theory]]. Such a field theory would have to lift the Lorentz group to the [[special linear group]] <math>\text{SL}(2,\mathbb C)</math> as its [[spacetime symmetries|spacetime symmetry]] group, since the former does not admit [[spin representation|spinor representations]].<ref name="CFT"/>{{rp|117}} This is in contrast to the quantum theory which does admit spinor representations even when the spacetime symmetries are described by the Lorentz group. This is because the states in a Hilbert space are defined only up to a complex phase,<ref name="Weinberg1">{{cite book|first=S.|last=Weinberg|author1-link=Steven Weinberg|title=The Quantum Theory of Fields: Foundations|publisher=Cambridge University Press|date=1995|chapter=6|volume=|page=|isbn=9780521670531}}</ref>{{rp|81}} so particles belong to [[projective representation]]s rather than regular representations, with the projective representations of the Lorentz group being equivalent to regular representations of <math>\text{SL}(2,\mathbb C)</math>.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|176}} Classical spinor fields do not ordinarily arise as macroscopic classical fields in our universe because the [[Pauli exclusion principle]] prevents populating the field with a sufficient number of particles to reach the [[classical limit]].<ref name="CFT"/>{{rp|347}} However, many-fermion systems can often be described classically using fermion bilinears or collective observables, such as the current or the [[stress-energy tensor]].

== Properties ==

=== Lorentz transformations ===

The [[Lorentz group]] <math>\text{SO}(1,3)</math>, {{refn|group=nb|Strictly speaking the <math>\text{SO}^+(1,3)</math>, which is the part of the Lorentz group connected to the [[identity element|identity]]. It excludes [[parity (physics)|parity]] and [[T-symmetry|time-reversal]] transformations.}} describing the transformation between [[inertial frame of reference|inertial reference frames]], can admit many different [[representation theory|representations]].<ref name="Carmeli">{{cite book|last1=Carmeli|first1=M.|author-link1=Moshe Carmeli|last2=Malin|first2=S.|author-link2=|date=2000|title=Theory Of Spinors: An Introduction|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=World Scientific Publishing|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-9812564726}}</ref>{{rp|38}} A representation is a particular choice of [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] that [[faithful representation|faithfully]]{{refn|group=nb|A representation, mapping group elements <math>g \in G</math> to matrices <math>\rho(g) \in \text{GL}(V)</math>, is faithful if the mapping between group elements and matrices is [[injective function|injective]].}} represent the action of the [[group (mathematics)|group]] on some [[vector space]], which is sometimes referred to as a [[module (mathematics)|module]], where the [[dimension (vector space)|dimensionality]] of the matrices can differ between representations.<ref name="Keski">{{cite book|last1=Keski-Vakkuri|first1=E.|author-link1=|last2=Montonen|first2=C.|author-link2=|last3=Panero|first3=M.|author-link3=|date=2022|title=Mathematical Methods for Physics: An Introduction to Group Theory, Topology and Geometry|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Cambridge University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-1107191136}}</ref>{{rp|54}} For example, the Lorentz group can be represented by <math>4\times 4</math> real matrices <math>\Lambda</math> acting on the vector space <math>\mathbb R^{1,3}</math>, corresponding to how [[Lorentz transformation]]s act on vectors or on [[spacetime]].<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|159}} Another related representation is a set of <math>4\times 4</math> complex matrices acting on [[Dirac spinor]]s in the complex vector space <math>\mathbb C^4</math>.<ref name="Fradkin">{{cite book|last=Fradkin|first=E.|author-link=Eduardo Fradkin|date=2021|title=Quantum Field Theory: An Integrated Approach|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Princeton University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0691149080}}</ref>{{rp|24}} A smaller related representation is a set of <math>2\times 2</math> complex matrices acting on [[Weyl equation|Weyl spinor]]s in the <math>\mathbb C^2</math> vector space.<ref name="Srednicki">{{cite book|last=Srednicki|first=M.|author-link=|date=2007|title=Quantum Field Theory|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Cambridge University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0521864497}}</ref>{{rp|209}}

[[Lie group]] elements can be generated using the corresponding [[Lie algebra]], which together with a [[Lie bracket]], describes the [[tangent space]] of the group [[manifold]] around its identity element.<ref name="Osborn">{{cite web |last=Osborn|first=H.|date=|title=PART I: Symmetries and particles|url=https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/examples/3P2Lb.pdf|website=Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics|location=|publisher=University of Cambridge|access-date=November 16, 2025}}</ref>{{rp|64}} The [[basis (linear algebra)|basis elements]] of this vector space are known as [[generating set of a group|generators]] of the group. A particular group element is then acquired by [[matrix exponential|exponentiating]] a corresponding tangent space vector.<ref name="Aldrovandi">{{cite book|last1=Aldrovandi|first1=R.|author-link1=|last2=Pereira|first2=J.G.|author-link2=|date=1995|title=Introduction To Geometrical Physics|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=World Scientific Publishing|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-9810222321}}</ref>{{rp|295}} The generators of the Lorentz Lie algebra must satisfy certain [[anticommutative property|anticommutation]] relations, known as a Lie bracket. The six vectors can be packaged into an antisymmetric object <math>X^{\mu\nu}</math> indexed by <math>\{\mu,\nu\}</math>, with the bracket for the Lorentz algebra given by<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|39}}

:<math>
[X^{\mu\nu},X^{\rho\sigma}] = i(\eta^{\nu \rho}X^{\mu\sigma} - \eta^{\mu\rho}X^{\nu \sigma} + \eta^{\mu\sigma}X^{\nu \rho}-\eta^{\nu \sigma}X^{\mu\rho}).
</math>

This algebra admits numerous representation, where each generator is represented by a matrix, with each [[algebra representation]] generating a corresponding [[group representation|representation]] of the group.<ref name="Aldrovandi"/>{{rp|662}} For example, the representation acting on real vectors is given by the six matrices <math>X^{\mu\nu} = M^{\mu\nu}</math> where<ref name="Aldrovandi"/>{{rp|664}}

:<math>
\left(M^{\mu\nu}\right)^\rho{}_\sigma = i(\eta^{\mu\rho}\delta^\nu{}_\sigma - \eta^{\nu \rho}\delta^\mu{}_\sigma).
</math>

The Lorentz transformation matrix can then be acquired from these generators through an exponentiation<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|169}}

:<math>
\Lambda = \exp\left(\tfrac{i}{2}\omega_{\mu\nu}M^{\mu\nu}\right),
</math>

where <math>\omega_{\mu\nu}</math> is an antisymmetric matrix encoding the six [[degrees of freedom (physics and chemistry)|degrees of freedom]] of the Lorentz group used to specify the particular group element. These correspond to the three boosts and three [[rotation]]s.<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|40}}

Another representation for the Lorentz algebra is the [[spin representation|spinor representation]] where the generators are given by<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|169}}

:<math>
S^{\mu\nu} = \tfrac{i}{4}[\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu].
</math>

In this case the Lorentz group element, specified by <math>\omega_{\mu\nu}</math>, is given by

:<math>
S[\Lambda] = \exp\left(\tfrac{i}{2}\omega_{\mu\nu}S^{\mu\nu}\right).
</math>

The mapping of <math>\Lambda \mapsto S[\Lambda]</math> is not one-to-one since there are two consistent choices for <math>\omega_{\mu\nu}</math> that give the same <math>\Lambda</math> but a different <math>S[\Lambda]</math>.<ref name="Osborn"/>{{rp|45}} This is a consequence of the spinor representation being [[projective representation]]s of the Lorentz group <math>\text{SO}(1,3)</math>.<ref name="Weinberg1"/>{{rp|81}} Equivalently, they are regular representation of [[Special linear group|<math>\text{SL}(2,\mathbb C)</math>]], which is a [[Double cover (topology)|double cover]] of the Lorentz group.<ref name="CFT"/>{{rp|106}}

Under a Lorentz transformation, spacetime coordinates transform under the vector representation <math>x'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu x^\nu</math>, while the spinors transform under the spinor representation

:<math>
\psi'(x') = S[\Lambda]\psi(x).
</math>

The Dirac equation is a Lorentz covariant equation, meaning that it takes the form in all inertial reference frames.<ref name="Fradkin"/>{{rp|5}} That is, it takes the same form when for a spinor <math>\psi(x)</math> with [[coordinate system|coordinates]] <math>x</math>, as well as for a Lorentz transformed spinor <math>\psi'(x')</math> in the Lorentz transformed coordinates <math>x' = \Lambda x</math>

:<math>
(i{{\partial}\!\!\!/}'-m)\psi'(x') = 0,
</math>

where <math>\partial_\mu'</math> is the [[four-gradient]] for the new coordinates <math>x'</math>.{{refn|group=nb|The proof relies on the fact that [[gamma matrices]] satisfy the identity <math>S\left[\lambda^{-1}\right]\gamma^\mu S[\Lambda] = \Lambda^{\mu}{}_\nu \gamma^\nu</math>.}} Meanwhile, the Dirac action is Lorentz invariant, meaning that it is the same in all reference frames <math>S'=S</math>.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|166–168}}

=== Symmetries ===

Dirac's theory is invariant under a global <math>\text{U}(1)</math> [[symmetry (physics)|symmetry]] acting on the [[phase factor|phase]] of the spinor<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|174}}

:<math>
\psi(x) \rightarrow e^{i\alpha} \psi(x), \qquad \bar \psi(x) \rightarrow e^{-i\alpha} \bar \psi(x).
</math>

This has a corresponding [[conserved current]] that can be derived from the action using [[Noether's theorem]], given by<ref name="ASBook"/>{{rp|532}}

:<math>
j^\mu = \bar \psi \gamma^\mu \psi.
</math>

This symmetry is known as the vector symmetry because its current transforms as a [[vector (mathematics and physics)|vector]] under Lorentz transformations. Promoting this symmetry to a [[gauge theory|gauge symmetry]] gives rise to [[quantum electrodynamics]].

In the [[massless particle|massless limit]], the Dirac equation has a second inequivalent <math>\text{U}(1)</math> symmetry known as the [[axial current|axial symmetry]], which acts on the spinors as<ref name="Tong">{{Citation|last=Tong|first=D.|author-link=David Tong (physicist)|title=Quantum Field Theory|chapter=|date=2006|url=https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/qft.pdf}}</ref>{{rp|99}}

:<math>
\psi(x) \rightarrow e^{i\beta \gamma^5}\psi(x), \qquad \bar \psi(x) \rightarrow e^{i\beta \gamma^5}\bar \psi(x),
</math>

where <math>\gamma_5</math> is the chiral matrix. This arises because in the massless limit the Dirac equation reduces to a pair of [[Weyl equation]]s.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|168}} Each of these is invariant under a <math>\text{U}(1)</math> phase symmetry. These two symmetries can then be grouped into the vector symmetry where both Weyl spinors transform by the same phase, and the axial symmetry where they transform under the opposite signs of the phase.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|621}} The current corresponding to the axial symmetry is given by<ref name="ASBook"/>{{rp|532}}

:<math>
j^\mu_5 = \bar \psi \gamma^\mu \gamma^5 \psi.
</math>

This transforms as a [[pseudovector]], meaning that its spatial part is odd under parity transformations.<ref name="Srednicki"/>{{rp|469}} [[Classical physics|Classically]], the single-fermion axial symmetry admits a well-formulated gauge theory, but at the [[quantum mechanics|quantum level]] it has a [[chiral anomaly]] that provides an obstruction towards gauging.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|616}}

The spacetime symmetries of the Dirac action correspond to the [[Poincaré group]], a combination of spacetime [[translation (geometry)|translations]] and the Lorentz group.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|109}} Invariance under the four spacetime translations yields the Dirac [[stress-energy tensor]] as its [[four-current]]s<ref name="Tong"/>{{rp|98}}

:<math>
T^{\mu\nu} = i \bar \psi \gamma^\mu \partial^\nu \psi - \eta^{\mu\nu}\mathcal L_\text{Dirac},
</math>

where the last term is the Dirac Lagrangian, which vanishes [[on shell and off shell|on shell]]. Invariance under Lorentz transformations meanwhile yields a set of currents indexed by <math>\rho</math> and <math>\sigma</math>, given by<ref name="Tong"/>{{rp|99}}

:<math>
(\mathcal J^\mu)^{\rho \sigma} = x^\rho T^{\mu \sigma} - x^\sigma T^{\mu \rho} + \bar \psi \gamma^\mu S^{\rho \sigma}\psi,
</math>
where <math>S^{\rho \sigma}</math> are the spinor representation generators of the Lorentz Lie algebra, used to define how spinors transform under Lorentz transformations.

=== Plane wave solutions ===
{{Main|Plane-wave solutions to the Dirac equation}}

Acting on the Dirac equation with the operator <math>(i{{\partial}\!\!\!/} +m)</math> gives rise to the [[Klein–Gordon equation]] for each component of the spinor<ref name="Zee">{{cite book|last=Zee|first=A.|author-link=Anthony Zee|date=2003|title=Quantum Field Theory in a Nutshell|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Princeton University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0691010199}}</ref>{{rp|93}}

:<math>
(i{{\partial}\!\!\!/} +m)(i{{\partial}\!\!\!/} -m)\psi(x) = \left(\partial_\mu \partial^\mu + m^2\right)\psi(x) = 0.
</math>

As a result, any solution to the Dirac equation is also automatically a solution to the Klein–Gordon equation.<ref name="CFT"/>{{rp|349}} Its solutions can therefore be written as a [[linear combination]] of [[plane wave]]s.<ref name="Maggiore">{{cite book|last=Maggiore|first=M.|author-link=|date=2005|title=A Modern Introduction to Quantum Field Theory|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Oxford University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0198520740}}</ref>{{rp|59}}

The Dirac equation admits positive [[frequency]] plane wave solutions<ref name="Maggiore"/>{{rp|59}}

:<math>
\psi(x) = u(\boldsymbol p)e^{ip_\mu x^\mu}
</math>

with a positive energy given by <math>p_0 = \sqrt{\boldsymbol p^2+m^2}>0</math>. It also admits [[negative frequency]] solutions taking the same form except with <math>p_0 = -\sqrt{\boldsymbol p^2+m^2}<0</math>.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|188}} It is more convenient to rewrite these negative frequency solutions by flipping the sign of the momentum to ensure that they have a positive [[energy]] <math>p_0>0</math> and so take the form<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|48}}

:<math>
\psi(x) = v(\boldsymbol p)e^{-ip_\mu x^\mu}.
</math>

At the classical level these are positive and negative frequency solutions to a classical wave equation, but in the quantum theory they correspond to operators creating particles with spinor [[polarization (waves)|polarization]] <math>u(\boldsymbol p)</math> or [[creation and annihilation operator|annihilating]] [[antiparticle]]s with spinor polarization <math>v(\boldsymbol p)</math>.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|188}} Both these spinor polarizations satisfy the [[position and momentum space|momentum space]] Dirac equation<ref name="Maggiore"/>{{rp|59}}

:<math>
({{p}\!\!\!/} + m)u(\boldsymbol p) = 0,
</math>
:<math>
({{p}\!\!\!/} - m)v(\boldsymbol p) = 0.
</math>

Since these are simple matrix equations, they can be solved directly once an explicit representation for the gamma matrices is chosen. In the chiral representation the general solution is given by<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|190}}

:<math>
u(\boldsymbol p) = {\sqrt{p\cdot \sigma}\xi_s \choose \sqrt{p\cdot \bar \sigma}\xi_s}, \qquad v(\boldsymbol p) = {\sqrt{p\cdot \sigma}\eta_s \choose - \sqrt{p\cdot \bar \sigma}\eta_s},
</math>

where <math>\xi_s</math> and <math>\eta_s</math> are arbitrary complex 2-vectors, describing the two spin degrees of freedom for the particle and two for the antiparticle.<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|45}} In the massless limit, these spin states correspond to the possible [[helicity (particle physics)|helicity]] states that the massless fermions can have, either being [[chirality (physics)|left-handed]] or right-handed.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|190}}

== Related equations ==

=== Related Dirac equations ===

While the standard Dirac equation was originally derived in a <math>3+1</math> dimensional [[spacetime]], it can be directly generalized to arbitrary [[dimension]] and [[metric signature]]s, where it takes the same covariant form.<ref name="Dong">{{cite book|last=Dong|first=S.|author-link=|date=2011|title=Wave Equations in Higher Dimensions|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-9400719163}}</ref>{{rp|51}} The crucial difference is that the [[gamma matrices]] must be changed to gamma matrices of the [[Clifford algebra]] appropriate in those dimensions and metric signature, with the size of the [[Dirac spinor]] corresponding to the dimensionality of the gamma matrices. While the Dirac equation always exists, since every dimension admits Dirac spinors, the properties of these spinors and their relation to other [[spin representation|spinor representations]] differs significantly across dimensions.<ref name="Freedman"/>{{rp|59}} Other differences include the absence of a [[chirality (physics)|chirality matrix]] in odd dimensions.<ref name="ASBook"/>{{rp|534}}

The equation can also be generalized from flat [[Minkowski space]]time to [[curved spacetime]] through the introduction of a spinor [[covariant derivative]]<ref name="Freedman"/>{{rp|179}}

:<math>
D_\mu = \partial_\mu - \tfrac{i}{4}\left(\omega_{\alpha \beta}\right)_\mu \gamma^\alpha \gamma^\beta,
</math>

where <math>\omega_{\alpha \beta}</math> is the [[spin connection]] that can be defined using the [[tetrad formalism]]. The [[Dirac equation in curved spacetime]] then takes the form<ref name="Ortin">{{cite book|last=Ortin|first=T.|author-link=|date=2015|title=Gravity and Strings|url=|doi=|location=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press|chapter=5|pages=175–186|edition=2|isbn=978-0521768139}}</ref>{{rp|862}}

:<math>
(i\gamma^\mu D_\mu -m)\psi(x) = 0.
</math>

Adding self-interaction terms to the Dirac action gives rise to the [[nonlinear Dirac equation]], which allows for the [[fermion]]s to interact with themselves, such as in the [[Thirring model]].<ref name="KorepinB">{{cite book|last=Korepin|first=V.|author-link=Vladimir Korepin|date=2010|title=Quantum Inverse Scattering Method and Correlation Functions|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Cambridge University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0521586467}}</ref>{{rp|81}} Interactions between fermions can also be introduced through [[electromagnetism|electromagnetic]] effects. In particular, the [[Breit equation]] describes multi-electron systems interacting electromagnetically to first order in [[Perturbation theory (quantum mechanics)|perturbation theory]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Breit|first1=G.|authorlink1=Gregory Breit|date=1929|title=The Effect of Retardation on the Interaction of Two Electrons|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.34.553|journal=Phys. Rev.|volume=|issue=34|pages=553–573|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.34.553|pmid=|arxiv=|s2cid=|access-date=|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The [[two-body Dirac equation]] is a similar multi-body equation.

A [[geometry|geometric]] reformulation of the Dirac equation is known as the Dirac–Hestenes equation.<ref name="Rodrigues">{{cite book|last1=Rodrigues|first1=W.A.|author-link1=Waldyr Alves Rodrigues Jr.|last2=Oliveira|first2=E.C.|author-link2=|date=2010|title=The Many Faces of Maxwell, Dirac and Einstein Equations: A Clifford Bundle Approach|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Springer|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-3642090387}}</ref> In this formulation all the components of the Dirac equation have an explicit geometric interpretation. Another related geometric equation is the [[Dirac–Kähler equation]], which is a geometric analogue of the Dirac equation that can be defined on any general [[pseudo-Riemannian manifold]] and which acts on [[differential form]]s.<ref name="Montvay">{{cite book|last1=Montvay|first1=I.|last2=Munster|first2=G.|date=1994|title=Quantum Fields on a Lattice|series=Cambridge Monographs on Mathematical Physics|url=|doi=10.1017/CBO9780511470783|location=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press|chapter=4|pages=205–207|isbn=9780511470783|s2cid=118339104 }}</ref> In the case of a [[flat manifold]], it reduces to four copies of the Dirac equation. However, on curved manifolds this decomposition breaks down and the equation fundamentally differs.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Banks|first1=T.|author-link1=|last2=Dothan|first2=Y.|author-link2=|last3=Horn|first3=D.|title=Geometric fermions |author-link3=|date=1982|url=|journal=Phys. Lett. B|volume=117|issue=6|pages=413–417|doi=10.1016/0370-2693(82)90571-8|pmid=|arxiv=|bibcode=1982PhLB..117..413B |s2cid=|access-date=}}</ref> This equation is used in [[lattice field theory]] to describe the continuum limit of [[staggered fermion]]s.

=== Weyl and Majorana equations ===

The Dirac spinor can be decomposed into a pair of Weyl spinors of opposite chirality <math>\psi^T = (\psi_L,\psi_R)</math>.<ref name="CFT"/>{{rp|340}} Under [[Lorentz transformation]]s, one transforms  as a left-handed Weyl spinor <math>\psi_L</math> and the other as a right-handed Weyl spinor <math>\psi_R</math>. In the chiral representation of the gamma matrices, the Dirac equation reduces to the pair of equations for the Weyl spinors<ref name="Maggiore"/>{{rp|57}}

:<math>
i\sigma^\mu \partial_\mu \psi_R(x) = m\psi_L(x),
</math>
:<math>
i \bar \sigma^\mu \partial_\mu \psi_L(x) = m\psi_R(x).
</math>

In particular, in the [[massless particle|massless]] limit the Weyl spinors [[coupling (physics)|decouple]] and the Dirac equation is equivalent to a pair of [[Weyl equation]]s.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|168}}

This decomposition has been proposed as an intuitive explanation of [[Zitterbewegung]], as these massless components would propagate at the [[speed of light]] and move in opposite directions, since the [[Helicity (particle physics)|helicity]] is the projection of the [[spin (physics)|spin]] onto the direction of [[motion]].<ref name="PenroseZigzag">{{cite book |last1=Penrose |first1=Roger |title=The Road to Reality |date=2004 |publisher=Alfred A. Knopf |isbn=0-224-04447-8 |pages=628–632 |edition=Sixth Printing}}</ref> Here the role of the [[mass]] is not to make the [[velocity]] less than the speed of light, but instead controls the [[average]] rate at which these reversals occur; specifically, the reversals can be modelled as a [[Poisson process]].<ref name="PRL_1984_07_30">{{cite journal |last1=Gaveau |first1=B. |last2=Jacobson |first2=T. |last3=Kac |first3=M. |last4=Schulman |first4=L. S. |title=Relativistic Extension of the Analogy between Quantum Mechanics and Brownian Motion |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=30 July 1984 |volume=53 |issue=5 |pages=419–422|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.53.419 |bibcode=1984PhRvL..53..419G }}</ref>

A closely related equation is the [[Majorana equation]], with this formally taking the same form as the Dirac equation except that it acts on Majorana spinors.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|193}} These are spinors that satisfy a reality condition <math>\psi = C \bar \psi^T</math>, where <math>C</math> is the [[C symmetry|charge-conjugation operator]].<ref name="Freedman"/>{{rp|56}} In [[extra dimensions|higher dimensions]], the Dirac equation has similar relations to the equations describing other spinor representations that arise in those dimensions.

=== Pauli equation ===
{{Main|Pauli equation}}

In the non-relativistic limit, the Dirac equation reduces to the [[Pauli equation]],<ref name="Blundell"/>{{rp|332}} which when coupled to electromagnetism has the form

:<math>
\left[\frac{1}{2m}\left(\boldsymbol \sigma \cdot (\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}-q \boldsymbol A)\right)^2+q\phi \right]|\psi\rangle = 0.
</math>

Here <math>\boldsymbol \sigma</math> is the vector of [[Pauli matrices]] and <math>\hat{\boldsymbol p} = -i\nabla</math> is the [[momentum operator]]. The equation describes a fermion of [[electric charge|charge]] <math>q</math> coupled to the [[electromagnetic field]] through a [[magnetic vector potential]] <math>\boldsymbol A</math> and an [[electric potential|electric scalar potential]] <math>\phi</math>.<ref name="Davyadov"/>{{rp|258}} The fermion is described through the two-component [[wave function]] <math>|\psi\rangle</math>, where each component describes one of the two spin [[quantum state|states]] <math>|\psi\rangle = \psi_+|\uparrow\rangle + \psi_-|\downarrow\rangle</math>.<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|711}}

The Pauli equation is often used in [[quantum mechanics]] to describe phenomena where [[theory of relativity|relativistic effects]] are negligible but the spin of the fermion is important.<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|711–715}} It can also be recast in a form which directly shows that the [[gyromagnetic ratio]] of the fermion described by the Dirac equation is exactly <math>g=2</math>.<ref name="Maggiore"/>{{rp|74}} In [[quantum electrodynamics]] there are additional quantum corrections that modify this value, give rise to a non-zero [[anomalous magnetic dipole moment|anomalous magnetic moment]].<ref name="BJBook"/>{{rp|712}}

== Gauge symmetry ==

=== Vector symmetry ===

The vector and [[axial current|axial symmetries]] of the Dirac action are both global [[symmetry (physics)|symmetries]], in that they act the same everywhere in [[spacetime]].<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|34}} In [[classical field theory]], the [[Lagrangian (field theory)|Lagrangian]] can always be modified in a way to elevate a global symmetry to a local symmetry, which can act differently at different spacetime locations.<ref name="CFT"/>{{rp|166–167}} In the case of the vector symmetry, which corresponding to a global change of the [[spinor]] [[field (physics)|field]] by a [[phase factor|phase]] <math>\psi \rightarrow e^{i\alpha}\psi</math>, [[gauge theory|gauging]] would result in an [[action (physics)|action]] invariant under a local symmetry where the phase can take different values at different points <math>\psi \rightarrow e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi</math>.<ref name="Maggiore"/>{{rp|70}} While symmetries can always be gauged in classical field theory, this may not always be possible in the full [[quantum mechanics|quantum theory]] due to various obstructions such as [[anomaly (physics)|anomalies]], which signal that the full quantum theory is not invariant under the local symmetry despite its classical Lagrangian being invariant.<ref name="Fradkin"/>{{rp|177}} For example, the axial symmetry in the [[massless particle|massless]] Dirac theory with one [[fermion]] is anomalous due to the [[chiral anomaly]] and cannot be gauged.<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|661}}

Elevating the vector symmetry to a local symmetry means that the original action is no longer invariant under the symmetry due to the appearance of a <math>\partial_\mu \alpha(x)</math> term arising from the [[kinetic term]].<ref name="CFT"/>{{rp|167}} Instead, a new field <math>A_\mu(x)</math>, known as a gauge field, must be introduced. It must also transform under the local symmetry as<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|78}}

:<math>
A_\mu \rightarrow A_\mu + \tfrac{1}{e}\partial_\mu \alpha,
</math>

where <math>e</math> plays the role of the [[electric charge|charge]] of the [[Dirac spinor]] to the gauge field. The Dirac action can then be made invariant under the local symmetry by replacing the derivative term with a new [[gauge covariant derivative]]<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|173}}

:<math>
D_\mu\psi = \partial_\mu \psi +ie A_\mu\psi.
</math>

The Dirac action then takes the form<ref name="Maggiore"/>{{rp|71}}

:<math>
S = \int d^4x \bar \psi(i{{D}\!\!\!\!/}-m)\psi = \int d^4 x \left[\bar \psi(i{{\partial}\!\!\!/} - m)\psi -ej^\mu A_\mu\right].
</math>

This result can also be directly acquired through the Noether procedure, which is the general principle that a global symmetry can be gauged through the introduction of a term coupling the gauge field to the appropriate global symmetry [[four-current|current]].<ref name="CFT"/>{{rp|161}} Additionally introducing the kinetic term for the gauge field results in the action for [[quantum electrodynamics]].<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|78}}

=== General symmetries ===

The symmetries that can be gauged can be greatly expanded by considering a theory with <math>N</math> [[indistinguishable particles|identical]] Dirac spinors <math>\psi^a</math> labelled by a new [[index notation|index]] <math>a</math>. Together these spinors can be considered as being part of a single object <math>\psi</math> with components <math>\psi^{i,a}</math> where <math>i</math> labels the four spin components, and <math>a</math> the different spinors.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|491}} The largest global symmetry of this action is then given by the [[unitary group]] <math>\text{U}(N)</math>.<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|490}}

Any continuous [[subgroup]] of <math>\text{U}(N)</math> can then be gauged. In particular, if one wishes to gauge the symmetry acting on all <math>N</math> components, then the symmetry being gauged must admit an <math>N</math>-dimensional [[unitary representation]] acting on the spinors.<ref name="Srednicki"/>{{rp|420}} That is, for every <math>g \in \text{G}\subseteq \text{U}(N)</math>, there exists an <math>N\times N</math> dimensional matrix [[group representation|representation]] <math>\rho(g)</math> such that

:<math>
\psi(x) \rightarrow \rho(g)\psi(x)
</math>

forms a [[faithful representation]] of the [[group (mathematics)|group]]. Gauging the largest continuous subgroup, <math>\text{SU}(N)</math>, requires the spinors to transform in the [[fundamental representation|fundamental]] or [[antifundamental representation]].<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|484}}{{refn|group=nb|Gauging a larger dimensional representation of <math>\text{SU}(N)</math> with representation dimension <math>M</math> requires instead considering <math>M</math> identical spinors and gauging the <math>\text{SU}(N) \subset \text{U}(M)</math> subgroup.}} Gauging elevates the representation from being spacetime independent to being spacetime dependent <math>\rho(g(x))</math>.<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|490}} It requires introducing a gauge field <math>A_\mu^a</math>, formally the [[connection (principal bundle)|connection]] on the [[principal bundle]],<ref>{{cite book|last=Nakahara|first=M.|author-link=|date=2003|title=Geometry, Topology and Physics|url=|doi=|edition=2|location=|publisher=CRC Press|chapter=|pages=377–380|isbn=978-0750306065}}</ref> which necessarily transforms in the [[adjoint representation]] of the [[gauge group (mathematics)|gauge group]]. The covariant derivative then takes the form<ref name="CFT"/>{{rp|223}}

:<math>
D_\mu \psi = \partial_\mu \psi + \tilde \rho (A_\mu)\psi.
</math>

One symmetry that frequently gets gauged is the [[special unitary group]] <math>\text{SU}(N)</math> symmetry. Spinors transforming in the fundamental representation transform as<ref name="Srednicki"/>{{rp|416}}

:<math>
\psi(x) \rightarrow U(x)\psi(x),
</math>

where <math>U(x)</math> is a <math>N \times N</math> [[unitary matrix]] corresponding to a particular group element. The gauge field is a matrix valued gauge field <math>A^a_\mu</math> which transforms in the adjoint representation as<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|492}}

:<math>
A_\mu(x) \rightarrow U(x)A_\mu(x) U^{-1}(x) + \frac{1}{g}(\partial_\mu U(x))U^{-1}(x).
</math>

The covariant derivative then takes the form

:<math>
D_\mu \psi = \partial_\mu \psi + i g A_\mu \psi.
</math>

By also introducing the kinetic term for the gauge field, one constructs the action for [[quantum chromodynamics]]<ref name="Peskin"/>{{rp|489}}

:<math>
S_{\text{QCD}} = \int d^4 x \left[-\tfrac{1}{4}\text{Tr}(F^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}) + \bar \psi(i{{D}\!\!\!/} -m)\psi\right],
</math>

where in the gauge field kinetic term, the [[Yang–Mills theory|Yang–Mills fields]] [[gluon field strength tensor|strength tensor]] is defined as

:<math>
F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu - ig [A_\mu, A_\nu].
</math>

The case of <math>\text{SU}(3)</math> describes strong interactions of the [[quark]] sector of the [[Standard Model]], with the gauge field corresponding to [[gluon]]s and the Dirac spinors to the quarks.<ref name="Burgess">{{cite book|last1=Burgess|first1=C.|author-link1=|last2=Moore|first2=G.|author-link2=|date=2006|title=The Standard Model: A Primer|url=|doi=|location=|publisher=Cambridge University Press|chapter=|page=|isbn=978-0521860369}}</ref>{{rp|54}} The <math>\text{SU}(2)</math> case also plays a role in the Standard Model, describing the [[electroweak theory|electroweak sector]]. The gauge field in this case is the [[W-boson]], while the Dirac spinors are [[lepton]]s.<ref name="Schwartz"/>{{rp|592}}
